To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the thermal response of skin to millimeter‐wave energy depends on the thermal properties of the subcutaneous tissues, and that the thermal resistance of fat and muscle layers may be the dominant contributor to the temperature rise in skin even when the energy is absorbed almost entirely in the superficial layers.
the increase in temperature of the skin surface is determined by the thermal properties of the subcutaneous tissues and not the RF energy absorption in the skin.

the thermal response of tissue to RF exposure at frequencies above 10 GHz is determined by the thermal properties of the subcutaneous layers and not the RF energy deposition in the skin layer; and, that the thermal response can be accurately predicted by a 3‐layer skin model (Derm, Fat, Muscle) that assumes RF energy is absorbed in the skin layer only.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing a better understanding of the thermal effects of RF exposure above 6  GHz.
developing a better understanding of the thermal response of skin to RF exposure at frequencies above 10 GHz.
the development of models that can be used to predict the temperature elevation of human skin exposed to millimeter‐wave energy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the current exposure guidelines for RF fields at frequencies above 100 MHz are not based on a sufficient understanding of the thermal response of human tissue to RF energy.
the skin temperature elevation is a function of both the absorbed power density and the thermal properties of the tissue.
the current RF exposure guidelines are not protective against the potential health hazards from exposure to RF fields above 6  GHz.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in the frequency range above 6 GHZ, where energy penetration is limited to the outermost layers of the skin (stratum corneum, viable epidermal, and dermal layers), the increase in temperature is determined primarily by the thermal resistance (or heat transport capacity) of the subcutaneous fat.
we have developed a new model that is able to describe the thermal response of skin to millimeter‐wavelength radiation and to explain the experimental data.

the RF energy absorption is limited to the skin layers (the first 1–2 mm of skin) but the temperature increase is largely determined by the heat transport properties of the deeper layers of skin and the subcutaneous fat.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the thermal response of tissues to RF exposure above 6 GHz is determined by the thermal properties and thickness of subcutaneous layers, and not by the RF energy absorption in the skin layer.
the thermal response of human skin to exposure to millimeter waves is determined by the thermal properties of subcutaneous fat and muscle, not by the skin layers.
the thermal response of skin at frequencies above 10 GHz is determined primarily by the thermal conductivity of the subcutaneous tissue.
